items.title: 6.2.5 Intersection of a Line and a Circle

source_refs.note: Book p. 176-178: 6.2.5 line y = mx + c and circle x^2 + y^2 = a^2, discriminant Cases I-III, Corollary 1 (tangency), Corollary 2 (point of contact)

blocks.text:
Let the equation of the line be
\[y = mx + c \quad \text{...(1)}\]
and the equation of the circle be
\[x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2} \quad \text{...(2)}\]
The coordinates of the points of intersection are the simultaneous solutions of (1) and (2). Substituting the value of \(y\) from (1) into (2):
\[x^{2} + (mx + c)^{2} = a^{2}\]
\[x^{2} + m^{2}x^{2} + 2mxc + c^{2} - a^{2} = 0\]
\[x^{2}(1 + m^{2}) + 2mcx + (c^{2} - a^{2}) = 0 \quad \text{...(3)}\]
Equation (3) is a quadratic in \(x\) and gives two values of \(x\), say \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\). Corresponding to these values of \(x_{1}\) and \(x_{2}\), we get values of \(y\) as \(y_{1}\) and \(y_{2}\). Thus, the line \(y = mx + c\) intersects the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) in at most two points \((x_{1}, y_{1})\) and \((x_{2}, y_{2})\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why substitute? A point of intersection lies on both the line and the circle, so its coordinates satisfy both equations at the same time. Putting \(y = mx + c\) into the circle leaves one equation in \(x\) only.
Why "at most two"? Equation (3) is a quadratic (its leading coefficient \(1 + m^{2}\) is never 0), and a quadratic has at most two roots. Each real root \(x\) gives one point, with \(y\) from the line.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Recall: for \(Ax^{2} + Bx + C = 0\) the discriminant is \(B^{2} - 4AC\). Here \(A = 1 + m^{2}\), \(B = 2mc\), \(C = c^{2} - a^{2}\). Positive: two different real roots; zero: one repeated root; negative: no real root.
Case-I: Two distinct real points

The two points of intersection of the line \(y = mx + c\) and the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) are real and distinct, if the discriminant \(> 0\), that is, if
\[4[a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2}] > 0\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2} > 0\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) > c^{2}\]
Case-II: One real point (tangent)

The line \(y = mx + c\) touches the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) at only one real point, that is, the case of coincident points, if the discriminant \(= 0\), that is, if
\[4[a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2}] = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2} = 0\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) = c^{2}\]
Case-III: No real intersection

The line \(y = mx + c\) cuts the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) at two imaginary points (that is, does not cut the circle) if the discriminant \(< 0\), that is, if
\[4[a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2}] < 0\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2} < 0\]
\[\Rightarrow a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) < c^{2}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The three cases have a simple picture. The distance from the centre \((0, 0)\) to the line \(mx - y + c = 0\) is \(d = \frac{|c|}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\), so \(a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) \gtreqless c^{2}\) is the same as \(a \gtreqless d\):
\(d < a\): the line passes through the circle and cuts it twice (a secant).
\(d = a\): the line just touches the circle (a tangent).
\(d > a\): the line misses the circle.
Corollary-1: Condition of Tangency of a Line to a Circle

From Case II, the line \(y = mx + c\) is a tangent to the circle \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\) if:
\[|c| = a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}} \quad \text{or} \quad c = \pm a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\]
Therefore, the family of tangents to the circle is:

blocks.text_alt: y equals m x plus or minus a times the square root of 1 plus m squared

blocks.text:
Note that \(\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\) is the perpendicular distance from the centre \((0, 0)\) to the line.
Hence, the condition for tangency is that the distance \(\dfrac{|c|}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\) equals the radius \(a\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How to use \(y = mx \pm a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\): if the slope \(m\) of a tangent is known (for example, parallel or perpendicular to a given line, or inclined at a given angle), put \(m\) and the radius \(a\) in this formula; the \(\pm\) gives the two parallel tangents on opposite sides of the circle.
Our illustration (not from the book): tangents to \(x^{2} + y^{2} = 9\) with slope \(\frac{4}{3}\):
\[y = \dfrac{4}{3}x \pm 3\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{16}{9}}\]
\[y = \dfrac{4}{3}x \pm 5\]
Check: the distance from \((0, 0)\) to \(4x - 3y \pm 15 = 0\) is \(\frac{15}{5} = 3\), the radius.
The formula is only for a circle with centre at the origin. For any other circle use the same idea directly: distance from the centre to the line = radius.
Corollary 2: Coordinates of Point of Contact

For the tangent \(y = mx + a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\), the quadratic equation (3) has equal roots given by:
\[x = \dfrac{-2mc}{2(1 + m^{2})} = \dfrac{-mc}{1 + m^{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{-m}{1 + m^{2}}\left(a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\right)\]
\[= \dfrac{-am}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\]
Substituting into the equation \(y = mx + a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\):
\[y = m\left(\dfrac{-am}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\right) + a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{-am^{2}}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}} + a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\]
\[= \dfrac{-am^{2} + a(1 + m^{2})}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\]
\[= \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\]
Thus, the point of contact is
\[\left(\dfrac{-am}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}, \dfrac{a}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\right)\]
Similarly, for the tangent \(y = mx - a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\), the point of contact is
\[\left(\dfrac{am}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}, \dfrac{-a}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\right)\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \(x = \frac{-2mc}{2(1 + m^{2})}\)? When the discriminant is zero, the quadratic formula gives the single root \(x = -\frac{B}{2A}\).
Check on the circle: \(\frac{a^{2}m^{2}}{1 + m^{2}} + \frac{a^{2}}{1 + m^{2}} = a^{2}\). So the point is really on the circle.
The two points of contact are opposite ends of a diameter (one is the negative of the other), as expected for two parallel tangents.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. To find where a line meets a circle, substitute the line into the circle and solve the quadratic.
2. For \(y = mx + c\) and \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\): \(D = 4[a^{2}(1 + m^{2}) - c^{2}]\).
3. \(D > 0\): two points; \(D = 0\): tangent; \(D < 0\): no real point.
4. Tangency: \(c^{2} = a^{2}(1 + m^{2})\); tangents of slope \(m\): \(y = mx \pm a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\).
5. Point of contact of \(y = mx + a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\): \(\left(\frac{-am}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}, \frac{a}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\right)\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using \(c = \pm a\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}\) for a circle whose centre is not the origin.
2. Mixing the letter \(c\) of the line \(y = mx + c\) with the constant \(c\) of the general circle; in this section the circle is \(x^{2} + y^{2} = a^{2}\).
3. Dropping the \(\pm\): there are two tangents with a given slope.
4. Pairing the wrong point of contact with the tangent: for the \(+\) tangent the \(y\)-coordinate is \(+\frac{a}{\sqrt{1 + m^{2}}}\).
